result.question: Native mobile accessibility as a design decision, plus the current legal enforcement landscape for digital accessibility. Two halves. HALF ONE, native platform accessibility a DESIGNER must decide (not a developer): (1) Apple Dynamic Type — the text style ramp, what sizes the accessibility sizes reach, what a designer must commit to for a layout to survive the largest accessibility text sizes, and Apple's stated guidance on layouts that must reflow or switch to vertical at large sizes; (2) VoiceOver on iOS — accessibility traits, labels vs hints vs values, the rotor and heading structure, and what a designer decides about reading order and grouping; (3) Android TalkBack and the Android accessibility model — content descriptions, touch exploration, the recommended 48dp target and its relationship to WCAG, and Android font scaling including non-linear font scaling introduced in Android 14; (4) what accessibility requirements differ between native and web such that a web-derived checklist misses them entirely. HALF TWO, legal drivers and their CURRENT enforcement state as of 2026: (5) the European Accessibility Act (Directive EU 2019/882) — what became applicable in June 2025, exactly which products and services are in scope, the microenterprise exemption and its thresholds, and what conformance is measured against (EN 301 549 and its relationship to WCAG); (6) the US DOJ ADA Title II web rule (28 CFR part 35 subpart H) — the technical standard it names and its compliance deadlines by public entity size; (7) Section 508 and what standard it currently references; (8) whether any binding instrument yet names WCAG 2.2 rather than 2.1 or 2.0. Primary sources only: developer.apple.com HIG accessibility pages, developer.android.com accessibility docs, EUR-Lex directive text, ada.gov and the Federal Register, and ETSI EN 301 549. Reject law-firm marketing blogs and accessibility-vendor content marketing where a primary source exists.
result.summary: Split along the question's own seam: three platform-vendor queries (Apple HIG, Android docs, and the native-vs-web delta via W3C/standards bodies) and three regulatory queries (EU directive text, the EN 301 549 / harmonised-standard link, and US federal rulemaking including the WCAG 2.2 adoption question). Each query is pinned to a primary-source domain or document identifier so vendor SEO content and law-firm blogs rank below the authoritative text.

results.title: Features and APIs Overview — Android 14 (section: Non-linear font scaling to 200%)
results.snippet: The authoritative primary source for the Android 14 font-scaling change (subtopic 3). Verified quotes: max user font scale raised to 200%; "To prevent large text elements on screen from scaling too large, the system applies a nonlinear scaling curve... large text doesn't scale at the same rate as smaller text. Nonlinear font scaling helps preserve the proportional hierarchy between elements of different sizes while mitigating issues with linear text scaling at high degrees (such as text being cut off...)." Critical designer/dev trap documented here: "Don't use sp units for padding or define view heights assuming implicit padding: with nonlinear font scaling sp dimensions might not be proportional, so 4sp + 20sp might not equal 24sp." Also mandates android:lineHeight in sp, not dp, and points to TypedValue.applyDimension()/deriveDimension() for correct sp↔px conversion. This is the exact Android-vs-web divergence subtopic 4 asks about — web's rem/em scaling is linear, Android's is not above a threshold.

results.title: Accessibility — Mobile Design Guides | Android Developers
results.snippet: Google's designer-facing (not developer-facing) accessibility foundations page — the closest Android analogue to Apple's HIG accessibility pages, so it maps directly onto the question's "decisions a designer must make." Verified content: "Ensure all touch targets are at least 48 dp, even if this extends past the UI element visual" (filed under Design for motor skill / Switch Access, i.e. a design decision, not an implementation detail); minimum body text size 12 sp, aligned to the Material type scale; specify font size in sp so users can adjust it; contrast ratios 4.5:1 for text and 3:1 for surface-to-non-text elements; TalkBack described as "a Google screen reader included on Android devices that gives users eyes-free control"; and explicit reading-order guidance — "Consider UI granularity and group UI elements to allow skipping between blocks." Also links Material's Design-to-Implementation walk, which is where the WCAG cross-reference lives.

results.title: Principles for improving app accessibility | App quality | Android Developers
results.snippet: The canonical statement of the 48dp rule and its rationale: "For touch interfaces, we recommend that each interactive UI element have a focusable area, or touch target size, of at least 48dp x 48dp. An element such as an icon may appear to be 24dp x 24dp, but the padding surrounding it can make up the full 48 x 48 dp touch target." Note the framing as a *focusable area* independent of the visual — this is the key distinction from WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8 (24 CSS px minimum) and 2.5.5 (44 CSS px enhanced): Android's 48dp is stricter than WCAG's AA minimum and is a platform recommendation, not a legal conformance criterion. Also covers labels: "Each label must explain the semantics of a particular element — that is, the element's meaning and purpose," plus grouping related elements and exposing custom accessibility actions, which is the Android counterpart to VoiceOver traits/grouping decisions in subtopic 2.

results.title: Make apps more accessible | App quality | Android Developers
results.snippet: Google's top-level checklist page tying together the four things a designer signs off on: descriptive labels/content descriptions for every interactive element, adequate touch target size (48dp), sufficient contrast, and text that scales with the user's preference. Establishes the content-description model for subtopic 3 — labels are attached to elements via contentDescription (Compose Semantics) with decorative items explicitly set to null, which is a designer-authored content deliverable, not something a developer can infer. Useful as the entry point that distinguishes Android's semantics-tree model from the web's role/name/value ARIA model (subtopic 4): Android has no DOM, so traversal order and grouping are set by the semantics tree rather than source order.

results.title: Support user-scalable content | Jetpack Compose | Android Developers
results.snippet: Covers the layout consequence of non-linear scaling that a designer must plan for. Confirms Android's system scaling "applies a non-linear scale for better readability. Therefore, a zoomChange of 2.0 might not result in text that appears exactly twice as large." Distinguishes font scaling (only text grows, containers/padding/icons stay fixed) from display scaling, gives recommended in-app scale bounds (~0.75x to ~3.5x), and states the design requirement directly: "Test your UI against both in-app scaling and system-wide font or display settings. Check that your app's layouts adapt correctly without breaking, overlapping, or hiding content" — the Android parallel to Apple's guidance that layouts reflow or switch to vertical at large accessibility sizes (subtopic 1).

results.title: Test your app's accessibility (Explore your app with TalkBack) | Android Developers
results.snippet: Primary source for touch exploration / explore-by-touch behavior in subtopic 3 — the manual TalkBack walkthrough Google prescribes (swipe-to-next-element, explore-by-touch, and verifying focus order), plus the Accessibility Scanner tool. Relevant to the designer's reading-order and grouping decision because it defines what "correct order" is actually verified against on Android: linear traversal through the semantics tree with explore-by-touch as a spatial override. Linked as the recommended manual test from Google's own designer accessibility foundations page.

results.title: Typography — Apple Human Interface Guidelines
results.snippet: The canonical primary source for subtopic 1: Apple's own specification tables for the Dynamic Type text style ramp (Large Title, Title 1/2/3, Headline, Subhead, Body, Callout, Footnote, Caption 1/2) with point size, weight, and leading given per content size category — including the five accessibility categories AX1–AX5. Establishes 17pt Body as the default base, states the minimum recommended text size (11pt) and that system fonts scale automatically. This is the page a designer must read to commit to a type ramp rather than hard-coded point sizes, and the one that shows exactly how far the accessibility sizes push each style. Note the page is JS-rendered, so the size tables require loading in a browser rather than plain fetch.

results.title: Accessibility — Apple Human Interface Guidelines
results.snippet: Apple's top-level accessibility design guidance, covering both halves of the Apple angle. States the layout-survival rules directly: smaller side-by-side elements may overlap when enlarged, so wrap them onto a new line or lay them out vertically rather than horizontally; avoid overlapping text and excessive or unusable truncation; allow text to wrap to two or more lines instead of truncating; if text is truncated in a list, the full text must remain reachable in a detail view. Also carries the VoiceOver-facing design guidance (labels, traits, reading order, grouping) and the 44x44pt minimum hit target — the native counterpart to WCAG target-size criteria that a web-derived checklist expresses in CSS px.

results.title: VoiceOver — Apple Human Interface Guidelines
results.snippet: The dedicated HIG page for subtopic 2. Sets out the three-part model VoiceOver speaks for an element — label (a succinct localized name), trait (what the element's role/behavior is), and value (its current state) — plus hints as the optional fourth, spoken last and only when the outcome isn't obvious from the label. Critically for designers: labels must not include the control type ('button', 'checkbox') or state ('checked'), because those belong in traits/values and repeating them makes VoiceOver speak redundant information. Also covers the rotor as the navigation accelerator (headings, links, form controls, custom rotors), heading structure, reading order, and grouping related views into a single accessibility element so a card reads as one stop rather than five.

results.title: Get started with Dynamic Type — WWDC24 — Apple Developer Videos
results.snippet: Apple's most explicit statement of the reflow-to-vertical rule and the magnitudes involved. States that Dynamic Type on iOS exceeds 200% at AX3 and reaches over 300% body text at AX5 — the figure that shows why a WCAG 1.4.4 '200% resize' checklist is not sufficient on iOS. Demonstrates the designer-level decision as a concrete pattern: horizontal arrangements should switch to vertical stacking once an accessibility size is selected (AnyLayout swapping HStackLayout for VStackLayout in SwiftUI, or flipping UIStackView's axis in UIKit), so text gets full width and truncation is avoided. Also covers testing every screen at AX5 via Xcode Previews.

results.title: Larger Text evaluation criteria — Manage App Accessibility — App Store Connect Help
results.snippet: Apple's normative pass/fail criteria for declaring Larger Text support in an App Store Accessibility Nutrition Label — effectively the checklist Apple now measures Dynamic Type support against, which makes it more binding than HIG prose. Names the required test range (small, medium, large, and extra-large accessibility sizes), requires no overlapping or clipped text, and sets the truncation rule: truncation is acceptable only where the full text remains reachable elsewhere. Useful as the audit criteria a designer's spec must satisfy, distinct from the design guidance itself.

results.title: VoiceOver evaluation criteria — Manage App Accessibility — App Store Connect Help
results.snippet: The VoiceOver counterpart to the Larger Text criteria, stating the label/trait/value split as a testable requirement rather than advice: every element must expose a label that identifies it, a trait that speaks its type, and a value where state is conveyed only visually (e.g. a checked box). Directly supplies the native-vs-web gap in subtopic 4 — traits are an iOS-specific concept with no direct ARIA one-to-one mapping, and the requirement that state changes be announced is enforced through UIAccessibility notifications rather than aria-live, so a web checklist misses it entirely.

results.title: Extension of Compliance Dates for Nondiscrimination on the Basis of Disability; Accessibility of Web Information and Services of State and Local Government Entities (DOJ interim final rule, 89/91 FR, published April 20, 2026)
results.snippet: THE critical current-state document, and the one most secondary sources get wrong. DOJ interim final rule extending both Title II web-rule compliance dates by one year: entities with total population 50,000 or more move from April 24, 2026 to April 26, 2027; entities under 50,000 and ALL special district governments move from April 26, 2027 to April 26, 2028. The technical standard is unchanged — WCAG 2.1 Level AA. Any answer citing 'April 2026' as a live deadline is now out of date. Public-inspection PDF mirror at https://public-inspection.federalregister.gov/2026-07663.pdf (binary; the Federal Register HTML is the readable version, though federalregister.gov and ecfr.gov both 302-redirect to an unblock interstitial from some clients).

results.title: Nondiscrimination on the Basis of Disability; Accessibility of Web Information and Services of State and Local Government Entities (DOJ final rule, 89 FR 31320, April 24, 2024)
results.snippet: The originating rule itself — the primary text creating 28 CFR part 35 subpart H (§§ 35.200–35.205). Names WCAG 2.1 Level AA (W3C Recommendation 5 June 2018) as the technical standard, incorporated by reference, and covers both web content AND mobile applications — the only US federal instrument that explicitly reaches native mobile apps, which is the direct legal hook for the native-accessibility half of the question. Contains the preamble discussion of why 2.1 was chosen over 2.0 and over 2.2. Compliance dates in the original text (April 24, 2026 / April 26, 2027) are superseded by the 2026 extension above; everything else stands.

results.title: Fact Sheet: New Rule on the Accessibility of Web Content and Mobile Apps Provided by State and Local Governments | ADA.gov
results.snippet: DOJ's own plain-language fact sheet, and confirmed already updated to the post-extension dates: WCAG 2.1 Level AA; 50,000+ population by April 26, 2027; under 50,000 and special district governments by April 26, 2028. Also enumerates the five exceptions a designer needs to know are NOT blanket outs — archived content, pre-existing documents (Word/PDF/spreadsheet/presentation), third-party posts not under contract, password-protected individualized documents, and pre-existing social media posts — while noting the underlying effective-communication and reasonable-modification duties survive every exception.

results.title: Revised 508 Standards and 255 Guidelines | U.S. Access Board
results.snippet: Primary source for subtopic 7. The Revised 508 Standards (final rule January 18, 2017; correction January 22, 2018) incorporate WCAG 2.0 Level A and AA by reference — see E205.4 (electronic content), E207.2 (software), 602.3 (support documentation), and the incorporation-by-reference at 702.10.1. Still WCAG 2.0, not 2.1, not 2.2. Includes the safe harbor: ICT that complied with the original 2000 standards and was not altered after January 18, 2018 need not be modified. Note the version gap this creates — federal agencies under Section 508 are held to an older baseline than state/local governments under ADA Title II.

results.title: Section 508 ICT Testing Baseline Portfolio — Baseline for Web | U.S. Access Board
results.snippet: Directly answers subtopic 8 from a government source rather than a vendor blog: Section 508 does NOT incorporate WCAG 2.2; the Baseline tests reference the WCAG 2.2 versions of the Understanding articles only for clearer explanation of existing requirements, not to impose the nine new 2.2 success criteria. Combined with the Title II rule naming 2.1 and EN 301 549 tracking 2.1, this supports the conclusion that as of mid-2026 no binding US instrument names WCAG 2.2 — it appears in guidance and test methodology only.

results.title: Accessibility of Web Content and Mobile Apps Provided by State and Local Government Entities: A Small Entity Compliance Guide | ADA.gov
results.snippet: DOJ's required small-entity guide, useful for the mechanics a designer actually hits: how 'total population' is measured for the two-tier deadline (it is the population of the jurisdiction the entity serves, which is why special district governments are handled separately and always land in the later tier), what counts as a covered mobile app, and the conformance-vs-nonconformance test where minor deviations that do not affect access are not violations. Overlaps the fact sheet on the headline dates; its value is the edge-case sizing and scoping detail.

results.title: Guidance on Applying WCAG 2.2 to Mobile Applications (WCAG2Mobile) — W3C Draft Group Note
results.snippet: The W3C Mobile Accessibility Task Force's direct answer to subtopic 4. Published as a Draft Note May 2025, it covers native iOS/Android, mobile web, and hybrid apps. Core remapping: "the unit of conformance in WCAG 2 is a single web page" but "the equivalent unit of conformance for mobile applications is a single screen" — so "web page(s)" becomes "screen(s)/view(s)" and "set of web pages" becomes "set of screens." "Programmatically determined/associated" is restated as "accessibility services provided by platform software" (i.e. UIAccessibility / Android AccessibilityNodeInfo), and SC 1.4.11 / 1.4.13 substitute "user agent or platform software" where WCAG names only a user agent. It flags that web terminology "may not directly translate to mobile environments" and that applying web-derived criteria to native apps "has led to inconsistencies, confusion, and even conflict" — the exact failure mode of a web-derived checklist. Mobile-specific SCs it centers: 1.3.4 Orientation, 1.4.10 Reflow, 2.5.1 Pointer Gestures, 2.5.2 Pointer Cancellation, 2.5.4 Motion Actuation, 2.5.7 Dragging Movements, 2.5.8 Target Size (24x24 dp/pt, AA); 4.1.1 Parsing is obsolete/removed with an erratum on its limited native applicability; 1.4.4/1.4.12 tie to platform-level scaling such as Dynamic Type. Note: several sections still marked "Work In Progress," and it is informative, not normative.

results.title: Guidance on Applying WCAG 2 to Non-Web Information and Communications Technologies (WCAG2ICT) — W3C Group Note
results.snippet: The single most load-bearing source for "which web SCs simply do not exist in native." Directly quotes which criteria regulators have ruled inapplicable: "some local standards such as Section 508 in the U.S., and EN 301 549 in Europe, state that WCAG 2.0 Success Criteria 2.4.1 Bypass Blocks, 2.4.5 Multiple Ways, 3.2.3 Consistent Navigation, and 3.2.4 Consistent Identification do not apply to non-web documents and non-web software. In addition, EN 301 549 states that 2.4.2 Page Titled and 3.1.2 Language of Parts do not apply to non-web software." Term replacements: "web page" → "document"/"software"; "set of web pages" → "set of documents"/"set of software programs"; "user agent" redefined. It defines "accessibility services of platform software" as "services provided by an operating system, user agent, or other platform software that enable non-web documents or software to expose information about the user interface and events to assistive technologies" — the concept that replaces web DOM/ARIA semantics with VoiceOver traits and TalkBack content descriptions. Caveat it states about itself: it "does not specifically say which criteria can or should apply"; that determination is left to regulators. Bridges directly into Half Two: it is the mechanism by which EN 301 549 and Section 508 apply WCAG to native software at all.

results.title: Mobile Accessibility: How WCAG 2.0 and Other W3C/WAI Guidelines Apply to Mobile — W3C Group Note
results.snippet: The predecessor note WCAG2Mobile is built on, and still the most concrete on designer-level decisions that no web checklist contains. Recommends touch targets "at least 9 mm high by 9 mm wide" with surrounding inactive space — a physical-size rule, notably different from WCAG 2.2's 24x24 CSS px and from Apple's 44pt / Android's 48dp conventions, useful for showing that the web number and the platform numbers are not the same rule. Also covers: grouping operable elements that perform the same action to enlarge the effective target; simple vs complex touchscreen gestures needing discoverable on-screen indicators; device-manipulation gestures (shake, tilt) requiring touch/keyboard alternatives; screen-reader users' difficulty with multi-touch; supporting both portrait and landscape and exposing orientation change programmatically; virtual keyboard type selection per field; external and alternative keyboard support; honoring system-level text resizing, zoom, magnification and caption settings, with reflow when platform zoom raises text size; and placing critical content before the scroll point on small screens.

results.title: WCAG2ICT Overview — W3C Web Accessibility Initiative
results.snippet: Plain-language framing of WCAG2ICT and the bridge between the two halves of the question. States the Note applies WCAG principles and Level A/AA criteria to "mobile apps, native applications, platform software, and software on ICT with closed functionality," and provides "replacements for web-based language in WCAG success criteria and definitions," noting that "not all non-web software has a user agent or platform software with accessibility APIs." Confirms WCAG2ICT is "a key resource for including WCAG in ICT accessibility regulation" and that EN 301 549 is among the standards that use or reference it. Current version is based on WCAG 2.2 and was updated 21 January 2026 — a data point for the question of whether any binding instrument names WCAG 2.2, since WCAG2ICT itself is a Note (non-normative) and the binding force comes from EN 301 549 / Section 508 referencing it.

results.title: WCAG2ICT — W3C Group Note updated to coordinate with EN 301 549 (W3C WAI news, 21 Aug 2025)
results.snippet: Timeline evidence for subtopic 8 (does anything binding yet name WCAG 2.2). W3C states the August 2025 WCAG2ICT update was made "in coordination with the work to update EN 301 549," and the updated Note is the WCAG 2.2-based edition (wcag2ict-22). This shows the EN 301 549 revision toward WCAG 2.2 was in progress with W3C alignment during 2025, while the version in force under the European Accessibility Act at its June 2025 application date remained the earlier EN edition harmonized to WCAG 2.1 AA. Points to a changelog ("Changes since the 15 November 2024 Note") for substantive edits — worth fetching directly if the exact deltas matter.

results.title: Mobile Accessibility at W3C — W3C Web Accessibility Initiative
results.snippet: Authoritative index page establishing which W3C resource governs native apps and their current status: WCAG2Mobile ("Guidance on Applying WCAG 2.2 to Mobile Applications") described as an in-progress draft; WCAG2ICT as "a more general resource that also includes mobile apps"; and mobile-accessibility-mapping as the older WCAG 2.0-era resource. Scopes mobile accessibility beyond phones to tablets, digital TVs, wearables, car dashboards and IoT, and names the environmental and interaction challenges (touchscreens, small screens, speech input). Useful mainly for citing document status and precedence. Important negative finding for the research: this page does not mention VoiceOver, TalkBack, or platform accessibility APIs at all — confirming that W3C material alone cannot supply subtopics 1-3, which must come from developer.apple.com HIG and developer.android.com.

claims.claim: Apple states that iOS Dynamic Type reaches sizes larger than 200% of the default at the AX3 accessibility size, and allows body text sizes over 300% at AX5 — giving designers concrete numeric targets for the top of the Dynamic Type ramp.
claims.quote: Many accessibility guidelines recommend allowing users to enlarge text to 200% or larger than the default size. Dynamic Type on iOS, for example, reaches sizes larger than 200% at the AX3 size, and allows body text sizes over 300% at the AX5 size.

claims.claim: Apple's stated layout guidance for large accessibility text sizes is that side-by-side elements should reflow — wrapping onto a new line or being laid out vertically instead of horizontally — because they overlap when enlarged.
claims.quote: Smaller side-by-side elements may overlap when enlarged, so consider wrapping them onto a new line or laying them out vertically rather than horizontally.

claims.claim: Apple's criteria treat truncation as a failure condition at large text sizes: text must not truncate to the point of being unreadable or ambiguous, and the recommended remedy is wrapping to two or more lines.
claims.quote: Avoid truncating text to the point that it becomes unreadable or ambiguous for the user. Consider allowing the text to wrap to two or more lines instead of truncation.

claims.claim: Apple explicitly disallows relying on system-provided magnification (Zoom, Hover Text) to satisfy the Larger Text requirement — the app's own layout must scale, which is a native-specific requirement with no direct web-checklist equivalent (browser zoom/reflow is normally an acceptable web mechanism under WCAG 1.4.4/1.4.10).
claims.quote: Don't rely on system-provided assistive technology like _Zoom_ or _Hover Text_ to claim support for Larger Text.

claims.claim: The maximum Dynamic Type scale is platform-dependent rather than a single universal ramp: on watchOS the largest Dynamic Type size is larger than 140% of the default, versus the 200%+/300%+ figures cited for iOS.
claims.quote: Because Apple Watch has a smaller screen, the largest Dynamic Type size on watchOS is larger than 140% of the default size.

result.publishDate: Not stated on page; content is current as of 2026 (it references a WWDC 2026 session, \"Prepare your tvOS apps for Dynamic Type\")

claims.claim: Apple's Dynamic Type ramp offers 7 text sizes by default, plus 5 additional "larger accessibility sizes" when the user enables them, for 12 total sizes an app layout must survive.
claims.quote: By default, there are 7 available text sizes to chose from. If larger accessibility sizes is enabled, 5 more text sizes become available.

claims.claim: Apple's stated guidance is that horizontal layouts should dynamically switch to a vertical stack at accessibility text sizes so each element can take the full display width — a layout decision, not a font-size decision.
claims.quote: When the text size increases, the layout dynamically switches to a vertical stack allowing each cell to take the entire width of the display.

claims.claim: Apple instructs that when text scales, essential content should be scaled in preference to decorative views — i.e. decorative imagery should not scale with Dynamic Type, and text should wrap around it instead.
claims.quote: This is because apps should prioritize scaling essential content over decorative views.

claims.claim: For controls that structurally cannot grow with larger text (e.g. tab bars), Apple's prescribed native remedy is the Large Content Viewer rather than letting the control scale, exposed via .accessibilityShowsLargeContentViewer in SwiftUI and UILargeContentViewerItem / UILargeContentViewerInteraction in UIKit.
claims.quote: The Large Content Viewer allows you to explore controls that may not be able to grow with larger text sizes.

claims.claim: Apple frames Dynamic Type support as detectable by tooling: Xcode Previews' Dynamic Type Variants and accessibility audits surface clipped text at large sizes, meaning "survives the largest accessibility sizes" is a testable acceptance criterion, not a subjective one.
claims.quote: Run accessibility audits to detect clipped text, missing labels, and contrast issues

result.publishDate: June 2024 (WWDC24, session 10074; no explicit day shown on the page)

claims.claim: Apple states VoiceOver reads elements in the reading order of the user's active language and locale (top-to-bottom, left-to-right in US English), which means default reading order is derived from layout — so a designer must explicitly group related elements or VoiceOver will read all images before all captions rather than pairing each image with its caption.
claims.quote: VoiceOver reads elements in the same order people read content in the their active language and locale. For example, in US English, this is top-to-bottom, left-to-right. In the ungrouped example below, VoiceOver describes each image before moving on to the captions. In the grouped example, VoiceOver describes each image with its respective caption.

claims.claim: Apple assigns the grouping/ordering/linking of interface elements as an explicit design responsibility, instructing designers to audit the UI for relationships that are conveyed by visual cues only (proximity, alignment) and then describe those relationships to VoiceOver.
claims.quote: Specify how elements are grouped, ordered, or linked. Proximity, alignment, and other visible contextual cues help sighted people perceive the relationships between elements. Examine your app for places where relationships among elements are visual only. Then, describe these relationships to VoiceOver.

claims.claim: The VoiceOver rotor is a navigation control that lets people move through content by headings, links, and other content types, and Apple states apps must identify those elements to the rotor for it to work; the rotor can also bring up the braille keyboard.
claims.quote: Support the VoiceOver rotor when possible. People can use an interface element called the VoiceOver rotor to navigate a document or webpage by headings, links, and other content types. You can help people navigate content in your app by identifying these elements to the rotor. The rotor can also bring up the braille keyboard.

claims.claim: Apple designates the screen/page title as the first information an assistive technology conveys on arrival, and requires unique titles plus accurate section headings so users can build a mental model of the information hierarchy — making heading structure a per-screen design commitment, not a developer detail.
claims.quote: Use titles and headings to help people navigate your information hierarchy. The title is the first information someone receives from an assistive technology when arriving on a page or screen in your app. Offer unique titles that succinctly describe each page's content and purpose. Likewise, use accurate section headings that help people build a mental model of each page's information hierarchy.

claims.claim: A native-only requirement absent from any web accessibility checklist: on visionOS, turning VoiceOver on causes apps that define custom gestures to stop receiving hand input by default, unless the user opts into Direct Gesture mode — so custom-gesture interactions must have a non-gesture path.
claims.quote: Be mindful that custom gestures aren't always accessible. When VoiceOver is turned on in visionOS, apps and games that define custom gestures don't receive hand input by default. This ensures people can explore the interface using their voice, without an app responding to hand input at the same time. A person can opt out of this behavior by enabling Direct Gesture mode, which disables standard VoiceOver gestures and lets apps process hand input directly.

claims.claim: Android's official design guidance sets a minimum touch target of 48 dp, and explicitly requires that minimum be met even when it exceeds the visible bounds of the UI element.
claims.quote: Ensure all touch targets are at least 48 dp, even if this extends past the UI element visual.

claims.claim: Android requires font sizes to be declared in scalable pixels (sp) so user font-size settings apply, and sets a floor of 12 sp for body text aligned to the Material type scale.
claims.quote: To allow users to adjust the font size, specify font size in scalable pixels (sp) ... Don't make the body size any smaller than 12 sp. This guideline aligns with the Material typescale as a default.

claims.claim: Android's designer-facing accessibility guidance requires textual descriptions for icons and images, and requires decorative items to have their description set to null so screen readers skip them — a labelling decision distinct from web alt-text conventions.
claims.quote: To satisfy Android framework requirements, provide additional textual description of icons and images. ... Set decorative item descriptions to null.

claims.claim: Android specifies contrast ratios of at least 4.5:1 for text against background and 3:1 for non-text elements against surfaces, matching WCAG 2.x thresholds rather than defining a platform-specific number.
claims.quote: Ensure the contrast between the background and text is at least 4.5:1. ... Use a 3:1 ratio between surfaces and non-text elements. For example, the ratio of a background to an icon would be 3:1.

claims.claim: Android requires that gesture-driven interactions have non-gesture equivalents exposed as accessibility actions — a native-only requirement with no direct equivalent in a web-derived WCAG checklist.
claims.quote: Don't rely on gestures to complete all actions; create accessibility actions to support all user flows in your app.

claims.claim: Apple's iOS/iPadOS Dynamic Type ramp has 7 standard sizes (xSmall through xxxLarge, default = Large) plus 5 larger accessibility sizes AX1-AX5, and the Body text style scales from 17pt at the default to 53pt at AX5 - roughly 3.1x. Large Title runs 34pt to 60pt over the same range.
claims.quote: Large (default) … Body | Regular | 17 | 22 | Semibold … iOS, iPadOS larger accessibility type sizes … AX5 … Body | Regular | 53 | 62 | Semibold

claims.claim: Apple explicitly instructs designers to switch to a stacked (vertical) layout at large font sizes, naming inline glyphs, timestamps and container boundaries as the specific elements that crowd text and cause truncation or overlap in horizontally constrained contexts.
claims.quote: Consider adjusting your layout at large font sizes. When font size increases in a horizontally constrained context, inline items (like glyphs and timestamps) and container boundaries can crowd text and cause truncation or overlapping. To improve readability, consider using a stacked layout where text appears above secondary items.

claims.claim: Apple sets a concrete, testable commitment for surviving the largest accessibility sizes: the amount of useful text displayed at the largest accessibility font size should equal what is displayed at the largest standard font size, and truncation in scrollable regions is disallowed unless a separate full-content view exists.
claims.quote: Keep text truncation to a minimum as font size increases. In general, aim to display as much useful text at the largest accessibility font size as you do at the largest standard font size. Avoid truncating text in scrollable regions unless people can open a separate view to read the rest of the content.

claims.claim: Apple directs designers to reduce the number of text columns as font size increases, treating multicolumn layout as a size-dependent design decision rather than a fixed grid.
claims.quote: Multicolumn text can also be less readable at large sizes due to horizontal space constraints. Reduce the number of columns when the font size increases to avoid truncation and enhance readability.

claims.claim: Apple publishes per-platform default and minimum text sizes that apply to custom fonts as well as system fonts - iOS/iPadOS 17pt default / 11pt minimum, macOS 13/10, tvOS 29/23, visionOS 17/12, watchOS 16/12 - and names the exact Settings path designers must use to verify layouts at accessibility sizes.
claims.quote: Follow the recommended default and minimum text sizes for each platform — for both custom and system fonts … iOS, iPadOS | 17 pt | 11 pt … On iPhone or iPad, turn on Larger Accessibility Text Sizes in Settings > Accessibility > Display & Text Size > Larger Text, and confirm that your app remains comfortably readable.

result.publishDate: Last updated December 16, 2025 (per page change log; Dynamic Type guidance expanded March 7, 2025)

claims.claim: Android 14 raised the maximum user font scale to 200%, and applies a nonlinear scaling curve so large text scales less aggressively than small text — preserving type hierarchy and preventing cut-off or unreadably large display text.
claims.quote:
Starting in Android 14, the system supports font scaling up to 200%, providing users with additional accessibility options.

To prevent large text elements on screen from scaling too large, the system applies a nonlinear scaling curve. This scaling strategy means that large text doesn't scale at the same rate as smaller text. Nonlinear font scaling helps preserve the proportional hierarchy between elements of different sizes while mitigating issues with linear text scaling at high degrees (such as text being cut off or text that becomes harder to read due to an extremely large display sizes).

claims.claim: Because scaling is nonlinear, sp dimensions are no longer additive — 4sp + 20sp does not necessarily equal 24sp — so sp must not be used for padding or for view heights that assume implicit padding.
claims.quote: Don't use sp units for padding or define view heights assuming implicit padding: with nonlinear font scaling sp dimensions might not be proportional, so 4sp + 20sp might not equal 24sp.

claims.claim: Text sizes must be specified in sp units for the user's preferred text size to apply at all; apps using sp get the Android 14 scaling improvements automatically, but must still be UI-tested at the 200% maximum.
claims.quote: If you already use scaled pixels (sp) units to define text sizing, then these additional options and scaling improvements are applied automatically to the text in your app. However, you should still perform UI testing with the maximum font size enabled (200%) to ensure that your app applies the font sizes correctly and can accommodate larger font sizes without impacting usability.

claims.claim: Line height must be declared in sp, not dp or px; TextView only auto-corrects lineHeight to preserve intended proportions when both textSize and lineHeight are defined in sp.
claims.quote: Always define `android:lineHeight` using sp units instead of dp, so the line height scales along with your text. Otherwise, if your text is sp but your `lineHeight` is in dp or px, it doesn't scale and looks cramped. TextView automatically corrects the `lineHeight` so that your intended proportions are preserved, but only if both `textSize` and `lineHeight` are defined in sp units.

claims.claim: DisplayMetrics.scaledDensity is no longer accurate under Android 14 and Configuration.fontScale is informational only, because fonts are no longer scaled by a single scalar; conversions must go through TypedValue.applyDimension()/deriveDimension().
claims.quote: Avoid hardcoding equations using `Configuration.fontScale` or `DisplayMetrics.scaledDensity`. Because font scaling is nonlinear, the `scaledDensity` field is no longer accurate. The `fontScale` field should be used for informational purposes only because fonts are no longer scaled with a single scalar value.

results.title: Directive (EU) 2019/882 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 17 April 2019 on the accessibility requirements for products and services (full text, EUR-Lex)

Contains every provision subtopic 5 asks about: Art. 2 scope (product list — general-purpose computer hardware and OS, self-service terminals incl. payment terminals/ATMs/ticketing/check-in, consumer terminal equipment with interactive computing for electronic communications and audiovisual media services, e-readers; service list — electronic communications, access to AVMS, elements of air/bus/rail/waterborne passenger transport, consumer banking, e-books and dedicated software, e-commerce); Art. 3(23) microenterprise definition; Art. 4(5) exemption of microenterprises providing services; Art. 15 presumption of conformity via harmonised standards; Annex I essential accessibility requirements; Annex VI disproportionate-burden criteria; Art. 31 dates (in force 27 Jun 2019, transposition 28 Jun 2022, application 28 Jun 2025, with Art. 32 transitional periods to 28 Jun 2030 for service providers' pre-existing products and to 2045 for self-service terminals). Note: EUR-Lex blocked automated fetch during this run — cite it, but read the HTML in a browser to quote verbatim.

results.title: European Accessibility Act (EAA) — European Commission
results.snippet: Commission's own statement of scope and exemptions, useful as a citable plain-language gloss on the directive. States the microenterprise threshold in the legal form the user asked for: an enterprise employing fewer than 10 persons AND with annual turnover not exceeding EUR 2 million OR an annual balance sheet total not exceeding EUR 2 million. Confirms the exemption runs to microenterprises that provide *services* (product-side microenterprises are not exempt from the requirements themselves, only relieved of certain documentation duties). Also confirms the 28 June 2025 application date and the three-year compliance runway.

results.title: European accessibility act — Employment, Social Affairs & Inclusion, European Commission

Enumerates the covered products and services in the same order as Annex I and explains the selection rationale (products/services most important to persons with disabilities and most likely to diverge between Member States). Good cross-check on the Annex I product list — payment terminals, self-service terminals (ATMs, ticketing, check-in, interactive information terminals), smartphones and telecom-access equipment, TV equipment for digital TV services, and the transport-service elements (websites, mobile services, e-tickets, information).

results.title: ETSI EN 301 549 V3.2.1 (2021-03) — Accessibility requirements for ICT products and services (Harmonised European Standard, official PDF)
results.snippet: The standard text itself, answering the EN 301 549 ↔ WCAG relationship in subtopic 5 and feeding subtopic 8. V3.2.1 is the currently published version and incorporates WCAG 2.1 Level AA in full (clauses 9 web, 10 non-web documents, 11 software — clause 11 is the one that actually governs native mobile apps, mapping WCAG success criteria onto non-web software, which is exactly the native-vs-web gap in subtopic 4). Also carries clause 5 generic requirements and clause 13 ICT support services that have no WCAG equivalent at all.

results.title: ETSI Draft EN 301 549 V4.1.0 (2025-11) — Accessibility requirements for ICT products and services (draft for Public Enquiry/Vote)
results.snippet: Directly answers subtopic 8 — whether any binding instrument yet names WCAG 2.2. This is the draft revision that pulls in WCAG 2.2 Level AA; as of Aug 2026 it is still a *draft*, not the version cited in the Official Journal, so the standard that confers presumption of conformity under both the EAA and the Web Accessibility Directive remains V3.2.1 / WCAG 2.1 AA. Publication of V4.1.1 and its OJ citation are expected later, so the honest answer is: no binding EU instrument names WCAG 2.2 yet. (ETSI returned 403 to automated fetch; open in a browser.)

results.title: Accessibility of products and services — EUR-Lex legislative summary of Directive (EU) 2019/882
results.snippet: EUR-Lex's own official summary of 32019L0882. Condenses key dates (entry into force 27 June 2019, application from 28 June 2025) and the scope/exemption structure into a citable paragraph, which is handy for a design-facing document that needs one accurate sentence rather than the full Annex I text. Secondary to the full text, but it is a Publications Office document, not vendor content marketing.

results.title: ETSI EN 301 549 V3.2.1 (2021-03) — Harmonised European Standard: Accessibility requirements for ICT products and services
results.snippet: The actual standard text — the version currently in legal effect. Reproduces WCAG 2.1 Level A + AA success criteria in full inside clause 9 (web), clause 10 (non-web documents) and clause 11 (non-web software, i.e. native mobile apps), so the WCAG mapping is by direct incorporation, not by reference. Annex A (normative) maps clauses to the Web Accessibility Directive requirements; Table A.1 lists the applicable clauses for websites and Table A.2 for mobile applications. Note that native mobile apps are covered under clause 11 software requirements plus clause 5 generic and clause 6 two-way voice — the source for what a web-derived WCAG checklist misses. Also states that once cited in the OJEU under Directive 2016/2102, conformance with the normative clauses confers presumption of conformity with the corresponding essential requirements of that Directive.

results.title: Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/1339 of 11 August 2021 (OJ L 289, 12.8.2021) — amending Implementing Decision (EU) 2018/2048 as regards the harmonised standard for websites and mobile applications
results.snippet: The binding OJEU citation instrument. Names EN 301 549 v3.2.1 (2021-03) as the harmonised standard, replacing v2.1.2 (which had been cited by Implementing Decision (EU) 2018/2048). Confirms the citation is made under Directive (EU) 2016/2102 (Web Accessibility Directive) and against the essential requirements in Annex II of standardisation request C(2017) 2585 — i.e. this is the WAD harmonisation, not the EAA. Since v3.2.1 incorporates WCAG 2.1 AA, this is the instrument that makes WCAG 2.1 AA the operative EU benchmark. Directly answers subtopic 8 for the EU side: no EU instrument yet cites a version incorporating WCAG 2.2.

results.title: Draft ETSI EN 301 549 V4.1.0 (2025-11) — Harmonised European Standard (draft for Enquiry/Vote)
results.snippet: The primary source for the forthcoming version. This is the draft developed under Commission standardisation request M/587 (the EAA mandate) that incorporates WCAG 2.2 Level AA and adds separate mapping annexes so one standard can serve both Directive (EU) 2016/2102 and Directive (EU) 2019/882. Critical status point: it is a draft version number (V4.1.0 = draft; V4.1.1 would be the published Harmonised Standard), it is not yet published, and it is not yet cited in the OJEU — expected citation around late 2026. Read alongside V3.2.1 to see exactly which criteria WCAG 2.2 adds (2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured, 2.4.13 Focus Appearance is AAA, 2.5.7 Dragging Movements, 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) 24×24 CSS px, 3.2.6 Consistent Help, 3.3.7 Redundant Entry, 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication) and the removal of 4.1.1 Parsing. Note: server returns 403 to automated fetchers; open in a browser.

results.title: European Commission — Web accessibility standards: latest changes (Shaping Europe's digital future)
results.snippet: The Commission's own status page, last updated 30 June 2025 — authoritative confirmation that EN 301 549 v3.2.1 is the version currently referenced in the Official Journal, that it replaced v2.1.2 (cited 2018) in August 2021 with an overlap until February 2022, and that both versions 'build heavily on WCAG 2.1' with only small deltas because WCAG 2.1 itself did not change. Useful as the non-vendor, non-law-firm citation for 'which version is in force right now' without relying on the standard PDF.

results.title: Directive (EU) 2019/882 (European Accessibility Act) — consolidated text on EUR-Lex
results.snippet: The directive text itself, needed to close the loop on how conformance is measured. Article 15 sets the presumption-of-conformity mechanism: products and services in conformity with harmonised standards (or parts thereof) whose references have been published in the OJEU are presumed to conform to the accessibility requirements of Annex I, to the extent those standards cover them. Article 4 and Annex I define scope; Article 4(5) carries the microenterprise exemption for services (fewer than 10 persons and annual turnover/balance sheet total not exceeding EUR 2 million). The operative gap: because no harmonised standard has yet been cited in the OJEU *under this Directive*, Article 15's presumption is not yet available for the EAA — conformity must currently be demonstrated against Annex I directly, with EN 301 549 v3.2.1 / WCAG 2.1 AA used as de facto rather than presumptive evidence.

results.title: Commission Standardisation Request M/587 to CEN, CENELEC and ETSI in support of Directive (EU) 2019/882 (European Accessibility Act)
results.snippet: The mandate document that commissions the EAA-facing revision of EN 301 549 and defines its deliverables and deadlines — revised harmonised standards due 15 September 2025, new harmonised standards 15 March 2026 / 15 January 2027. Explains why V4.1.x exists and why it must map to two directives at once. Also shows the request covers more than ICT (EN 17210 built environment, EN 17161 Design for All, plus new work on non-ICT information and support services), which is why EN 301 549 alone does not cover the whole of EAA Annex I. This is the Commission's own text hosted on a CEPT server; the equivalent is retrievable from the Commission's standardisation request register.

claims.claim: Android's underlying font scaling system applies a non-linear scale, so a requested 2.0x zoom does not produce text exactly twice as large — meaning designers cannot assume linear proportionality between scale factor and rendered text size.
claims.quote: This approach leverages Android's underlying font scaling system, which applies a non-linear scale for better readability. Therefore, a `zoomChange` of 2.0 might not result in text that appears exactly twice as large, but it creates scaling behavior that is consistent with the user's system-wide accessibility settings.

claims.claim: Android documents a typical accessibility scale range of roughly 0.75x to 3.5x, giving designers a concrete upper bound their layouts must survive.
claims.quote: Note: For accessibility, typical min/max values are ~0.75x and ~3.5x.

claims.claim: Android states as research-backed guidance that content must reflow at large text sizes rather than require two-dimensional panning, because reflow is significantly more readable for low-vision users.
claims.quote: Research confirms that for users with low vision, reflowing content is significantly more readable and easier to navigate than interfaces that require two-dimensional panning.

claims.claim: Android distinguishes two scaling mechanisms a designer must design against separately: font scaling (fontScale) which grows only text while containers, padding, and icons stay fixed, versus density scaling which scales padding, spacing, and component sizes as well.
claims.quote: This strategy is more targeted, modifying only the `fontScale` factor. The result is that only text elements grow or shrink, while all other layout components—such as containers, padding, and icons—remain a fixed size.

claims.claim: Android requires testing layouts against both in-app scaling and system-wide font/display settings, with a pass criterion that layouts adapt without breaking, overlapping, or hiding content.
claims.quote: Build for all scales: Test your UI against both in-app scaling and system-wide font or display settings. Check that your app's layouts adapt correctly without breaking, overlapping, or hiding content.

claims.claim: Apple's App Store Connect VoiceOver evaluation criteria require a separate accessibility label distinct from the value for interactive form controls — the label names the field, the value carries its contents.
claims.quote: Buttons, icons, form controls, and all other elements should contain a concise label providing a text equivalent for VoiceOver users. Interactive text fields and similar form controls should have a label (for example, "phone number") in addition to the text value ("555-555-1212") of the selection or contents.

claims.claim: Apple explicitly prohibits encoding control type or state inside the accessibility label, and requires that information to be carried by accessibility traits instead — labels that duplicate the type produce doubled speech such as "checkbox, checkbox."
claims.quote: Ensure that labels don't include control types like "checkbox" or states like "checked." Otherwise, VoiceOver may speak redundant information to the user, such as "Unsubscribe checkbox, checkbox." Instead, implement these in your app as traits or through similar APIs appropriate to the device.

claims.claim: Apple's criteria require every visible element to be reachable both linearly (swipe/VO+Arrow) and via the VoiceOver rotor, require the user to be able to navigate away from any element, and require that forward and backward traversal never skip items or loop repeatedly.
claims.quote: VoiceOver users should be able to navigate to any visible element, either in order (swipe right, VO+Right, and so on) or by using a rotor and touch navigation on most platforms. […] VoiceOver users should be able to progress to each element without skipping items or looping back to the same item repeatedly. Try navigating forward through all contents, then backwards through all contents. Try looping through all rotor items forward and backwards, too.

claims.claim: For grouped elements, Apple gives designers a binary choice: either each item in the group is individually navigable, or the grouped behaviors are exposed as VoiceOver custom actions (e.g. reply, forward, delete on a single grouped row).
claims.quote: If multiple elements or actions are presented as a group, VoiceOver users should be able to either move to each item in the group, or be able to interact with the grouped behaviors (for example, reply, forward, delete) through features like custom actions.

claims.claim: Apple requires VoiceOver cursor/reading-position behavior that has no direct web equivalent: reading position must survive background content refresh, the cursor must move into newly presented content on screen change or modal presentation, and content behind an active modal must be unreachable.
claims.quote: When content reloads or refreshes in the background, a VoiceOver user's reading position shouldn't reset unexpectedly. […] When the screen changes or a modal dialog appears, the VoiceOver cursor should move logically into the new content area. VoiceOver users shouldn't be able to move into invisible, offscreen, or background content.

result.publishDate: Not stated — no publication or last-updated date is displayed on the page.

claims.claim: Android's official guidance sets a minimum focusable/touch target size of 48dp x 48dp for interactive UI elements on touch interfaces, with an explicit carve-out that precise input devices (mouse, trackpad) may use smaller targets. This is a dp-based platform recommendation stated independently of WCAG's CSS-pixel target-size criteria, and Material components (Button, IconButton, ListItem) enforce it by default in Compose.
claims.quote: For touch interfaces, we recommend that each interactive UI element have a focusable area, or _touch target size_, of at least 48dpx48dp. Larger is even better. ... **Note:** For precise input (mouses and trackpads), the touch target can be smaller. ... In Jetpack Compose, many built-in Material components like `Button`, `IconButton`, and `ListItem` already enforce this minimum size.

claims.claim: Android expresses its contrast thresholds against text sizes measured in sp (scale-independent pixels, the font-scaling unit), not px or pt: 4.5:1 is required below 18sp (or below 14sp bold), and 3:1 for all other text. Because sp values scale with the user's font-size setting, the size class a given text style falls into is not fixed at design time the way a web checklist assumes.
claims.quote: If the text is smaller than 18sp, or if the text is bold and smaller than 14sp, use foreground and background colors that result in a color contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1. For all other text, set the color contrast ratio to at least 3:1.

claims.claim: Android requires a designer-authored contentDescription per UI element that states purpose and outcome rather than visual appearance, must be unique per element, and must omit the control type (e.g. 'Submit', not 'Submit button') because the type is announced separately by the accessibility service — a labeling discipline with no direct web-checklist equivalent.
claims.quote: For each UI element in your app, include a description that describes the element's purpose. In most cases, you include this description in the element's `contentDescription` attribute ... Use descriptions to convey the purpose and result of the interaction, not the visual details. ... Avoid redundancies in descriptions. For example, if selecting a button causes a "submit" action to occur in your app, make the button's description `"Submit"`, not `"Submit button"`. ... Each description should be unique.

claims.claim: Android exposes element type to screen readers through an explicit Role semantics property (Role.Button, Role.Switch), the Android analogue to iOS accessibility traits — meaning a designer must decide the semantic role of every custom/composed control separately from its visual styling, since Compose surfaces have no implicit native role the way HTML elements do.
claims.quote: Use the `Role` semantics property (like `Role.Button` or `Role.Switch`) to expose a UI element's type. This way, screen readers can announce the element correctly.

claims.claim: Android instructs that purely decorative elements be explicitly marked with a null contentDescription so TalkBack skips them, and that Text composables need no contentDescription at all because the text itself is announced automatically — the native equivalent of the web's alt="" / aria-hidden decision, made per element at build time.
claims.quote: If a UI element has a `contentDescription` parameter but is purely decorative (such as an `Icon` that is part of another UI element), pass `null` to avoid redundant labeling. ... Note that you do not need to provide a `contentDescription` for `Text` composables. Android accessibility services (like TalkBack) automatically announce the text itself.

results.title: Federal Register: Extension of Compliance Dates for Nondiscrimination on the Basis of Disability; Accessibility of Web Information and Services of State and Local Government Entities (DOJ Interim Final Rule, 2026-07663)
results.snippet: THE CRITICAL 2026 UPDATE for subtopic 6, and it invalidates every pre-2026 write-up of this rule. DOJ published an interim final rule effective April 20, 2026 extending the Title II web/mobile compliance dates by one full year. The original deadlines (April 24, 2026 for entities of 50,000+; April 26, 2027 for smaller entities and special districts) are superseded by April 26, 2027 and April 26, 2028 respectively. The technical standard is unchanged: WCAG 2.1 Level AA. Any research output that still states an April 2026 deadline is wrong as of today. Note: federalregister.gov currently serves a bot-block redirect to unblock.federalregister.gov for automated fetches; the same document text is mirrored as a PDF at https://www.ada.gov/assets/pdfs/2026-ifr.pdf, which is directly retrievable.

results.title: eCFR — 28 CFR Part 35, Subpart H: Web and Mobile Accessibility
results.snippet: The binding codified regulatory text itself — the exact instrument named in subtopic 6, and the only citation that carries legal force rather than paraphrase. § 35.200 states the requirement and the two-tier compliance dates keyed to total population (50,000 threshold, with special district governments always in the later tier regardless of size); § 35.201 carries the five exceptions (archived web content, preexisting conventional electronic documents, third-party content not posted under contract, individualized password-protected documents, preexisting social media posts); § 35.202 covers conforming alternate versions; § 35.205 covers the minimal-impact non-conformance provision. WCAG 2.1 Level A and AA success criteria and conformance requirements are incorporated by reference — WCAG 2.2 appears nowhere in the text. Same bot-block caveat as federalregister.gov applies to automated fetching; a human browser reaches it fine.

results.title: ADA.gov — Fact Sheet: New Rule on the Accessibility of Web Content and Mobile Apps Provided by State and Local Governments
results.snippet: DOJ's own plain-language summary, and it has been updated to reflect the 2026 extension — it now states April 26, 2027 (population 50,000+) and April 26, 2028 (under 50,000 or any special district government). Answers subtopic 6 completely in one page: standard is WCAG 2.1 Level AA; mobile apps are explicitly and equally in scope alongside web content, on the same timeline with the same exceptions. Also documents exactly how the population threshold is computed — 2020 Census figures for most entities, with school districts resolved by district type (city districts use city population, county districts use county population, independent districts use Small Area Income and Poverty Estimates). Directly relevant to the native-mobile half of the question: this is the US instrument that puts native iOS/Android apps under a web-derived standard.

results.title: ADA.gov — Accessibility of Web Content and Mobile Apps Provided by State and Local Government Entities: A Small Entity Compliance Guide
results.snippet: The best primary source on the seam between the two halves of the research question: it confirms that native mobile apps ("software applications that are downloaded and designed to run on mobile devices") must meet WCAG 2.1 Level AA, while notably providing no technical translation layer for how a web-authored standard maps onto Dynamic Type, VoiceOver traits, or TalkBack content descriptions — which is itself the evidentiary basis for subtopic 4's claim that a web-derived checklist misses native requirements. Also states the two escape valves designers should know: equivalent facilitation (alternative designs permitted if provably equal-or-better accessibility) and conforming alternate versions (permitted only under genuine technical or legal limitation), plus the minimal-impact provision where a failure so minor it does not change a disabled person's access is not a violation.

results.title: Section508.gov — Applicability & Conformance Requirements (Revised 508 Standards)
results.snippet: Answers subtopic 7 directly and settles a common misconception. The Revised 508 Standards incorporate WCAG 2.0 Level AA by reference — not 2.1, not 2.2 — and apply those success criteria and conformance requirements to BOTH web and non-web electronic content, with the standards stating there is no distinction between web pages and non-web content because the same accessibility needs exist for all electronic content. That non-web extension (via E205 electronic content, E207/Chapter 5 §§501-504 software and authoring tools, plus the §§301-302 functional performance criteria) is the mechanism that pulls native mobile software into 508 scope. The 508 refresh final rule issued January 18, 2017 and took effect January 18, 2018; the baseline has not moved since.

results.title: U.S. Access Board — W3C WCAG 2.2 Now Available
results.snippet: The primary-source answer to subtopic 8, from the agency that would have to do the rulemaking. The Access Board acknowledges W3C's publication of WCAG 2.2 while stating that its Revised Section 508 Standards incorporate WCAG 2.0 by reference (IBR) — and it announces no rulemaking, no timeline, and no commitment to update that reference. Combined with the 28 CFR 35.200 text naming WCAG 2.1: as of August 2026 no binding US instrument names WCAG 2.2. The US enforcement floor is WCAG 2.0 AA for federal agencies and contractors under Section 508, and WCAG 2.1 AA for state and local government web content and mobile apps under ADA Title II. WCAG 2.2 in US federal solicitations is procurement preference or agency best practice, not a legal standard.

claims.claim: Android's TalkBack screen reader supports two distinct navigation models a designer must account for: sequential linear navigation (swipe right/left through elements in order) and touch exploration (drag a finger over the screen to hear what is under it), with double-tap-anywhere as the activation gesture in both.
claims.quote: Once TalkBack is on, there are two common ways to navigate: Linear navigation: quickly swipe right or left to navigate through screen elements in sequence. Double-tap anywhere to select the current screen element. Explore by tapping: drag your finger over the screen to hear what's under your finger. Double-tap anywhere to select the current element.

claims.claim: Google's official TalkBack review criteria are design-level, not code-level: they ask whether spoken feedback conveys each element's content or purpose, whether announcements are succinct rather than verbose, whether every element is reachable by swiping, and whether transient alerts are read aloud.
claims.quote: As you navigate, look for the following issues: Does the spoken feedback for each element convey its content or purpose appropriately? ... Are announcements succinct, or are they needlessly verbose? Can you complete the main workflows easily? Can you reach every element by swiping? If alerts or other temporary messages appear, are they read aloud?

claims.claim: Google Play runs automated accessibility tests on every uploaded app and reports findings in four categories — touch target size, low contrast, content labeling, and implementation — where 'implementation' explicitly includes traversal order that does not match the elements' logical arrangement.
claims.quote: Touch target size - Interactive elements in your app that have a focusable area, or touch target size, that is smaller than recommended. Low contrast ... Content labeling - UI elements that don't have a label that describes the elements' purpose. Implementation - Attributes assigned to UI elements that make it more difficult for the system's accessibility services to interpret the elements correctly—for example, using an element traversal order that doesn't match the elements' logical arrangement.

claims.claim: Android's own guidance states that static/automated analysis is insufficient: the Android Accessibility Test Framework in Android Studio cannot detect issues that surface only at runtime on a device, so manual exploration with TalkBack, Switch Access and Voice Access remains required.
claims.quote: Note: Keep in mind that the Android Accessibility Test Framework in Android Studio can't detect issues that occur when the app is running on a device.

claims.claim: This official Android accessibility-testing page never names WCAG, never states the 48dp minimum touch target figure, and gives no font-scaling test procedure — it describes touch targets only as 'smaller than recommended' and defers the numeric threshold to a separate linked page (/guide/topics/ui/accessibility/apps#large-controls).
claims.quote: Interactive elements in your app that have a focusable area, or touch target size, that is smaller than recommended.

claims.claim: Apple's HIG accessibility page sets an explicit text-enlargement target designers must design for: at least 200 percent enlargement (140 percent on watchOS), achievable either through custom UI or by adopting Dynamic Type.
claims.quote: **Support larger text sizes.** Make sure people can adjust the size of your text or icons to make them more legible, visible, and comfortable to read. Ideally, give people the option to enlarge text by at least 200 percent (or 140 percent in watchOS apps). Your interface can support font size enlargement either through custom UI, or by adopting Dynamic Type.

The quote is GENUINE and CURRENT — I verified it verbatim from the primary source (developer.apple.com HIG typography, fetched via https://developer.apple.com/tutorials/data/design/human-interface-guidelines/typography.json). It sits under the "Supporting Dynamic Type" section. But the CLAIM overstates the quote's normative force on two counts, and its thesis words are contradicted by the source's own wording.

(1) "concrete, testable commitment" is refuted by the quote itself. Apple writes "In general, aim to display as much useful text..." — a double hedge ("In general" + "aim to") against an undefined qualitative target ("useful text"). There is no threshold, no pass/fail criterion, no enforcement. Contrast with an actually testable instrument (WCAG 1.4.4 "resize up to 200 percent without loss of content or functionality"). Apple's line is aspirational guidance, not a commitment or a test.

(2) "truncation in scrollable regions is disallowed" is a modality fabrication. Apple's verb is "Avoid ... unless", in a guidelines document that is non-normative (HIG is not the App Review Guidelines; nothing here gates shipping). Confirmed by register check across the HIG: the adjacent accessibility page uses "aim to", "aim for", "Consider", "Strive to", "Avoid", "Prefer", "Ideally give people the option to enlarge text by at least 200 percent" — and contains NO "must", "required", or "shall" for text-size guidance. Every guidance sentence in the "Supporting Dynamic Type" section leads with Make/Increase/Keep/Consider/Maintain, i.e. recommendation verbs.

(3) "should equal" mis-paraphrases. Apple says "as much ... as you do" (a floor, plus the "In general, aim to" hedge), not an equality requirement.

(4) The claim also omits the sentence immediately following in the same paragraph, which is permissive and further undercuts "disallowed": "You can prevent text truncation in a label by configuring it to use as many lines as needed to display a useful amount of text."

Net: the factual content survives, the framing does not. A supported restatement would be: "Apple RECOMMENDS aiming to display as much useful text at the largest accessibility size as at the largest standard size, and to avoid truncation in scrollable regions unless a separate view exposes the rest." As written — "concrete, testable commitment" and "disallowed" — the claim converts hedged design guidance into a hard requirement and would mislead a designer about what is actually mandatory. Refuted as an overreach/misread of an otherwise authentic primary quote.
